title: Global Value Investing | Thomas Russo | Talks at Google
description:
“I consider myself to be a farmer—not a hunter. And I think most people on Wall Street are hunters. They like to fell big beasts and I’m very comfortable planting a few rows and just tending to them carefully.” - Thomas Russo

About the Talk
Mr. Russo looks forward to describing how that in his pursuit of long-term tax-deferred investment returns that he has favored investments in businesses whose global brands are well-position companies for reinvestment of mature market free cash flow into developing and emerging markets. Mr. Russo’s businesses accordingly possess the “capacity to reinvest” and managements who have the “capacity to suffer” when investments properly intended for longest term increase in intrinsic value on a per share basis burden as they often do, reported earnings in the near term. 

This tradeoff between near-term pain and long-term gain is at the heart of his investments when properly executed, the benefit for taxable investors is the ability to build portfolio companies whose return are long term and tax deferred. 

About the Speaker
Mr. Thomas A. Russo is the Managing Member of Gardner Russo & Gardner LLC, where he oversees $10 billion of “global value” equity investments invested through Semper Vic Partnerships as well as separately managed accounts. Mr. Russo is a Graduate of Dartmouth College (BA, 1977), and a Graduate of Stanford Business and Law Schools (MBA/JD, 1984). Memberships include Dean’s Advisory Council for Stanford Law School, Dartmouth College’s President’s Leadership Council, Heilbrunn Center for Graham & Dodd Investing (Columbia), Facing History and Ourselves, Winston Churchill Foundation of the United States, Storm King Art Center.
summary: The video argues that the capacity to suffer—defined as the ability to absorb short-term financial burdens or opportunity costs for long-term strategic goals—is a powerful driver of intrinsic value and long-term growth. This trait is observed in companies like Google and Amazon, which prioritize incubating projects or maintaining liquidity over immediate profit maximization. The speaker further illustrates this concept using Berkshire Hathaway, highlighting how Warren Buffett's focus on owner's equity and the willingness to incur costs (such as opportunity costs on cash or losses on new business) ultimately rewards shareholders.

claims.claim: Google has the capacity to suffer by incubating projects that burden profits, which is a powerful trait for long-term growth.
claims.quote: One is inside this room. You know, you think about all the kind of projects that Google incubates, burdening profit with an idea, maybe, of where it'll end up, but in some cases not even. That's extraordinarily powerful.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Amazon has a strong capacity to suffer and shareholders are rewarded for it despite potential lack of reported profits.
claims.quote: Amazon. Amazon's way out, even beyond you guys. I'm not sure that they'll ever report a profit. But they certainly have the capacity to suffer. So do their shareholders. Well, of course they get rewarded for it.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Berkshire Hathaway is the best example of a company with the capacity to suffer, allowing it to grow intrinsic value through reinvestment.
claims.quote: Berkshire is the best one. That's why I learned this subject. Warren talks about it all the time. But Geico's a great example. Much like confectionery in China, it's expensive, it turns out, to bring on an auto insured.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Warren Buffett controls a large portion of Berkshire stock and focuses on owner's equity and intrinsic value rather than manufacturing reported earnings.
claims.quote: Inside Berkshire, it didn't matter. Warren controls 40%+ of the stock. He's never told investors that he's in the business of manufacturing reported earnings. No one get stock options. He gets paid $100,000 a year.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Berkshire Hathaway added $20 billion of value to Geico since buying it by letting the income statement bear the burden of new insured costs.
claims.quote: And he said, for instance, at Geico we've added $20 billion of value since we bought it. Now that's that $20 billion that comes from those 9,000 new insured. And the only way you get there is by having the capacity to let the income statement bear the burden.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Warren Buffett kept $50 billion in cash earning low rates to avoid inflation risk, suffering a $2 billion annual opportunity cost to maintain liquidity.
claims.quote: Since he kept it in cash, he might as well keep it secure. But he was only making .01%. 01%. If he had standard company practices, he never would have kept $50 billion of cash in overnight money. He would have gone out three, 10, 14, 40 years on a bond portfolio and would have had a 4% yield.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Berkshire Hathaway sold a put option to insure a portfolio, receiving $5.3 billion to invest for 18 years despite mark-to-market charges.
claims.quote: He sold them a put option. In return, we received $5.3 billion to invest, unfettered, for 18 years. It was non-callable and it had no collateral posting requirements, which are the killers in this business.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Warren Buffett had $50 billion of spare cash which buttressed his claims-paying appeal and allowed him to honor obligations when others could not.
claims.quote: First, Warren had the capital. He had $50 billion of spare cash which sort of buttressed his claims-paying appeal. Other people who might take the $5 billion don't have the capital balance sheet or the culture to provide for the ultimate payment if the world went to zero and they owed $37 billion.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Berkshire Hathaway suffered a $2 billion annual opportunity cost by keeping cash in liquid treasuries rather than investing in longer-duration bonds.
claims.quote: The difference between 4% and 0.1% on $50 billion is $2 billion a year. That's the amount he suffered by under reporting, because he kept his money in liquid treasuries.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: Google incubates projects that may or may not end up succeeding, but the willingness to suffer for ideas is powerful.
claims.quote: You know, you think about all the kind of projects that Google incubates, burdening profit with an idea, maybe, of where it'll end up, but in some cases not even. That's extraordinarily powerful.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo

claims.claim: The speaker believes MasterCard has significant work ahead to convert cash to digital commerce, making it a worthy hold even if less undervalued now.
claims.quote: So it's expensive. It's gone up from $20 a share to $90 since I bought it in 2010. So at $90 it's not as compellingly undervalued, but I still think they have so much work ahead of them that it's a worthy hold.
claims.speaker: Thomas Russo
